# Writing Up the Survey {#sec-writing-up}

The last step turns the log into something another reader can use. This chapter shows the summary we wrote for this book.

## A timeline

Sorting the checked references by year shows when each line of work appeared.

| Year | Work | Line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1880 | @sprague1880 | Early theory |
| 1908 | @sprague1908 | History |
| 1965 | @ijiri1965 | Axioms |
| 1978 | @peters1978 | History |

| 1986 | @ellerman1986, @leech1986, @ijiri1986 | Groups, matrices, extensions |
| 1997 | @nehmer1997 | Algebraic models |
| 2000 | @arya2000 | Linear algebra |
| 2004 | @arya2004 | Linear algebra |
| 2005 | @rambaud2005 | Automata |
| 2008 | @katis2008 (written 1998) | Category theory |
| 2010 | @rambaud2010 | Algebraic models |
| 2014 | @ellerman2014 | Groups |
| 2021 | @stone2021 | History |
| 2023 | @liang2023, @ozawa2023matrix, @ozawa2023cashflow | Graphs, matrices |
| 2026 | @ozawa2026 | Monoids and groups |

The table lists only the works in this book's bibliography. It is not a complete history of the field.

## Where this book stands

The works in the timeline apply different areas of mathematics to bookkeeping: groups, algebraic models and automata, matrices, graphs, and categories. Part 0 shows that each of these areas has been applied to bookkeeping before. This book takes them one at a time, on a single running example, and checks its main theorems in Lean. A survey can show that a piece of work exists; a search that finds nothing is weaker evidence, because the work may exist under words we did not search for.

## Exercises

1. Build a timeline of the references in your log.
2. Write one paragraph that places your own project relative to the work you found. State what your search did not find, and how strong that evidence is.
3. For each claim in your paragraph, name the source in your log that supports it.
